S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.

subtypes.Skin Defects: Excessive preoccupation with practically invisible acne, scars, or complexion.
subtypes.Facial Features: Preoccupation with the shape or size of the nose, eyes, or mouth, which appear normal to others.
subtypes.Asymmetry: Excessive obsession with the face or body not being perfectly symmetrical.
subtypes.Muscle Dysmorphia: The belief that one's body is too small or insufficiently muscular despite being normal or muscular.
subtypes.Specific Body Parts: Obsession that specific parts like hair, teeth, or chest are ugly or abnormal.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.

subtypes.Mirror Checking or Avoidance: Compulsively checking oneself in the mirror frequently or, conversely, avoiding mirrors strictly.
subtypes.Excessive Camouflaging: Spending excessive time and effort to hide perceived flaws using makeup, clothes, hats, or sunglasses.
subtypes.Skin Picking: Picking or manipulating the skin excessively to remove or 'fix' flaws.
subtypes.Reassurance Seeking: Repetitively asking others for confirmation that one's appearance is okay or not strange.
subtypes.Comparing: Constantly comparing one's body parts with those of passersby or celebrities.
subtypes.Seeking Cosmetic Procedures: Repeatedly seeking or receiving plastic surgery or dermatological procedures.

symptom.disease_info: Body Dysmorphic Disorder is characterized by persistent preoccupation with one or more perceived defects in appearance that are absent or slight to others, accompanied by repetitive behaviors or mental acts such as checking, comparing, grooming, or seeking reassurance. It often has a chronic or fluctuating course, becomes clinically significant when distress or functional impairment develops, and is distinguished from normative appearance concerns by the intensity, repetitiveness, and interference it creates.

patient.stressor_event: Death of a close family member
patient.stressor: After the death of his father, Eric took responsibility for organizing family photographs, funeral arrangements, and a memorial slideshow, placing him face-to-face with images of himself beside relatives across many years. In that reflective period, he became increasingly fixed on a perceived facial imperfection and signs of aging that others described as barely noticeable, and he started spending more time checking his appearance before client meetings and mentally comparing himself with polished colleagues and gallery patrons. The problem remained outwardly contained, but it began to slow his morning routine, make him decline some art openings, and distract him during client-facing work enough that he recognized it as professionally inefficient and personally distressing. He raised it cautiously with his primary care physician during a routine visit and was referred for psychiatric assessment.

S067.name: Preoccupation_with_Appearance
S067.description: Preoccupation with one or more perceived defects or flaws in physical appearance that are not observable or appear slight to others.
S067.manifestation: What brings me in is that I keep getting stuck on this sagging, uneven look around my jaw and one side of my face, especially after seeing myself in all those family photos, even though my wife and clients say they barely notice anything.

S068.name: Appearance_Related_Repetitive_Behaviors
S068.description: Repetitive behaviors or mental acts performed in response to appearance concerns.
S068.manifestation: Before client meetings I’ll check the bathroom mirror and my phone camera several times, adjust the lighting, maybe change my collar or angle my face, and then I catch myself comparing my face to younger advisors or people at gallery events instead of focusing on the conversation.

add_requirements.functional_impairment: I still get through my work, but I’ve been slower getting out the door for client meetings, less present during some appointments, and I’ve skipped a few art openings because I didn’t want to be seen or photographed.
